definition: Browser isolation rules that restrict script access across origins. Ordinary HTTP(S) origins compare scheme, host and port; CORS can grant response sharing, while forms and some embeds may cross origins without exposing response data. Sending still depends on the applicable browser policies.
example: Script on https://blog.example can send a request to https://bank.example, but cannot read the reply unless the bank allows it with CORS.

definition: For ordinary HTTP(S) URLs, the normalized scheme, host and port used as a browser isolation boundary. Matching triples are same-origin; a differing component is cross-origin. Explicit default ports normalize to the omitted form; paths, queries and fragments do not affect the comparison.
example: https://shop.example/cart and https://shop.example/home are same-origin; http://shop.example is cross-origin because the scheme differs.

definition: An origin represented by a unique identity rather than a scheme/host/port tuple, used for contexts such as sandboxed documents without allow-same-origin. It serializes as null; distinct opaque origins are not equal, though a context can retain or inherit the same opaque-origin identity. Allowlisting null does not identify a particular trusted page.
example: Any website can create a sandboxed iframe whose requests carry Origin: null.

definition: For the domain-based HTTP(S) examples here, the scheme plus registrable domain used for same-site comparisons. HTTPS sibling subdomains can be same-site but cross-origin. Standards also define cases for hosts without a registrable domain and opaque origins; this simplified domain rule is not universal.
example: https://api.example.com and https://www.example.com are cross-origin but same-site.

definition: A public suffix plus one more label, such as example.com, or example.co.uk because co.uk is itself a public suffix. Written eTLD+1. Browsers use it, with the scheme, to decide what counts as the same site.
example: For https://www.shop.example.co.uk the registrable domain is example.co.uk.

definition: Effective top-level domain: a suffix under which the public can register names, such as .com, .co.uk or github.io. Browsers take these from the Public Suffix List. The registrable domain is the eTLD plus one more label.
example: Because github.io is a public suffix, alice.github.io and bob.github.io are different sites.

definition: A domain name nested under another, such as api.shop.example under shop.example. With different hosts the pages are cross-origin; with the same scheme and registrable domain they may be same-site. Cookie Domain rules may let a sibling set a parent-domain cookie, subject to prefix and other checks.
example: Under HTTPS, a compromised old-blog.example.com can be same-site with app.example.com without being same-origin.

definition: The part of a URL before its first colon, such as https, mailto or javascript, selecting how the URL is interpreted. Scheme is part of an ordinary HTTP(S) origin; other URL schemes can have opaque or scheme-specific origin rules.
example: In https://shop.example/cart the scheme is https.

definition: A number from 0 to 65535 that picks which service on a host a connection goes to. HTTPS uses 443 and HTTP uses 80 by default; writing the default explicitly does not change the origin, but any other port does.
example: https://shop.example and https://shop.example:443 are the same origin; https://shop.example:8443 is not.

definition: A URL host identifies its authority, commonly a domain name or IP address. Origin comparison uses the parsed, normalized host, so host case or equivalent IDN spelling is not compared as arbitrary raw text; a distinct subdomain normally differs.

The part of a URL after its fragment marker, exposed to page script through location.hash. It is excluded from an ordinary HTTP request target; client code can transmit it separately. Server response escaping alone does not transform a fragment on an independent client-side DOM path.
example: In /page#welcome, location.hash is "#welcome".

definition: An iframe with the sandbox attribute, which removes abilities such as running scripts unless keywords like allow-scripts grant them back. Without allow-same-origin the framed page gets an opaque origin that serialises as null. Any website can create one.
example: <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts" src="..."> runs script with Origin: null.

definition: An HTML element that embeds another web page inside the current one. Script in the parent cannot read a cross-origin iframe's content, and the two talk through postMessage. Clickjacking hides one under a decoy.
A flaw that reveals data an attacker should not see, such as a token, a secret page value or another user's response. Many web attacks need one as a first step.
example: A CSRF token copied into a URL can leak through logs or the Referer header.

definition: An HTTP name/value item stored with attributes after a Set-Cookie response. A browser may attach it to later matching requests in Cookie, subject to host/path, security, SameSite, credentials mode and other cookie policies. Attachment is not guaranteed on every later request.
example: An eligible same-origin authenticated request can carry Cookie: sid=abc after a server sets that cookie.

definition: In these examples, a cookie carrying a session identifier or signed session state. The server validates it under its authentication policy; possession alone does not establish user intent. The term also has a lifetime meaning: a cookie without a persistent expiry, whose session end and restoration depend on the user agent.
example: An eligible automatically attached authentication cookie can make an attacker-triggered form appear authenticated.

definition: The HTTP response header a server uses to create or update a cookie, with its name, value and attributes such as Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite and Path. Each cookie needs its own Set-Cookie line.
example: Set-Cookie: sid=abc; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

definition: An attribute following a cookie’s name and value in Set-Cookie. Domain and Path affect which requests match, while Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite impose further conditions. Domain scope and path matching do not provide the same isolation as web origins.
example: Omitting Domain makes a host-only cookie; Domain=example.com sends it to every subdomain too.

definition: A cookie attribute restricting sending to connections the user agent considers secure, ordinarily HTTPS. It does not encrypt the cookie at rest or prove the endpoint is trustworthy. SameSite=None and supported __Host-/__Secure- name rules require Secure; local-development exceptions depend on the client.

A cookie attribute preventing direct access through non-HTTP APIs such as document.cookie. Eligible cookies can still accompany requests made by injected same-origin script, so HttpOnly does not prevent all session abuse or theft paths.

A cookie attribute controlling cross-site sending, with Strict, Lax and None values. It can reduce classic CSRF but does not by itself isolate a same-site sibling origin, prove user intent or override other cookie restrictions.
example: SameSite=Lax stops a hidden cross-site form POST from carrying the session cookie.

definition: A SameSite value withholding the cookie on cross-site requests, including an initial navigation from a cross-site link. It is the most restrictive SameSite setting; the initial request can therefore appear unauthenticated when that cookie is the only session credential.

An explicit SameSite=Lax cookie is eligible for cross-site top-level navigations using safe methods, while other cross-site contexts are excluded by SameSite. Other cookie restrictions still apply. A browser’s default mode for an omitted attribute can have additional recent-cookie compatibility rules.
example: A cross-site form POST arrives without a Lax cookie; a cross-site link click to a GET page carries it.

definition: A SameSite value that puts no SameSite restriction on cross-site sending. The cookie must also be Secure, and browser third-party-cookie rules can still block it.

A version/configuration-dependent compatibility mode for recently created cookies with an omitted SameSite attribute. Chromium’s documented two-minute window can permit top-level cross-site unsafe navigations; explicit SameSite=Lax does not receive that default-mode exception. Other cookie conditions still apply.
example: A cookie created 60 seconds ago with no SameSite attribute still rides on a cross-site top-level POST.

definition: A cookie-name convention enforced by supporting clients. __Secure- requires Secure and a secure setting context; __Host- additionally requires Path=/ and no Domain, preventing a sibling host from setting that parent-host cookie. Cookies remain shared across ports on the same host.
example: __Host-csrf=... can only have been set by the exact host over HTTPS.

definition: A cookie used in a cross-site embedded or request context rather than the top-level site’s ordinary first-party context. Blocking, partitioning and exceptions vary by browser and configuration; SameSite=None alone does not guarantee sending.

Credentials automatically supplied under browser and authentication rules, such as eligible cookies, cached HTTP authentication or client certificates. Classic CSRF can abuse their eligible attachment. A bearer value manually added by application JavaScript is a different mechanism, even though both can use an Authorization header.
example: A session cookie is ambient; a bearer token that your JavaScript adds to an Authorization header is not.

definition: An attacker setting or overwriting a cookie in the victim's browser for your domain, for example from a sibling subdomain or by tampering with plain HTTP. It breaks naive double-submit CSRF defences, because the attacker chooses the cookie value.

HTTP Strict Transport Security: a learned or preloaded policy requiring secure transport for a host during its policy lifetime, optionally including subdomains. It mitigates network downgrade/injection on covered hosts; an unknown first visit, uncovered hosts and invalid certificates have separate rules.
example: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains asks for HTTPS-only for a year.

definition: Single sign-on: using an identity-provider authentication flow to access multiple applications. Some deployments involve cross-site POST navigations, one compatibility concern motivating Chromium’s recent-cookie default-SameSite exception.
The programming language that runs inside web pages. Script in a page can read and change the page and make requests, which is why getting attacker script to run (XSS) is so damaging.
Document Object Model: the browser's live tree of objects representing a page's elements, which script reads and changes. Reading a cross-origin iframe's DOM is blocked by the same-origin policy.

HyperText Markup Language: the tag-based language web pages are written in, such as

text

. Because a page is code, pasting untrusted text into it can change its structure.
Cascading Style Sheets: the language that styles web pages. Untrusted data inside CSS or a style attribute needs its own handling; it is best avoided.
fetch() is the browser's JavaScript function for making HTTP requests. The WHATWG Fetch Standard defines how browsers fetch everything, including CORS, preflights and when credentials are sent.
example: fetch("https://api.example/v1/orders", {credentials: "include"})

definition: XMLHttpRequest: the older browser API for making HTTP requests from script, before fetch(). It follows the same CORS rules; attaching upload progress listeners can force a preflight.

A Fetch setting controlling credential use and response credential handling: omit, same-origin by default, or include. Cross-origin eligible cookies require include, but SameSite and other policy can still exclude them; manually supplied authorization data is not simply synthesized by this setting.
example: fetch(url, {credentials: "include"}) asks for eligible cookies on a cross-origin request.

definition: A cross-origin request made with credentials mode include, so it may carry cookies. To let script read the response, the server must send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and name the exact origin, never *.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: HTTP headers with which a server tells the browser which other origins may read its responses, relaxing the same-origin policy. It also decides, through preflights, whether some requests may be sent. It is not server-side protection.
example: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://a.test lets script on https://a.test read the response.

definition: A request header the browser adds to CORS requests and many POSTs, naming the origin that started the request, such as Origin: https://a.test. Page script cannot set it, so servers use it for CORS decisions and CSRF checks; it can be null or missing.
The CORS response header naming the one origin allowed to read the response, or * for any origin. * is refused for credentialed requests, which need the exact origin.
example: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://a.test

definition: The CORS response header that, set to true, lets script read the response to a credentialed request. It only works together with an exact Access-Control-Allow-Origin value.
The preflight response header listing which HTTP methods the real request may use, such as DELETE.
The preflight response header listing which non-safelisted request headers the real request may carry, such as Authorization or x-token.
The preflight request header in which the browser says which method the real request will use, so the server can approve or refuse it.
The preflight request header in which the browser lists the non-safelisted headers the real request will carry.

A preflight response field giving a requested permission-cache lifetime in seconds. Fetch specifies five seconds for a missing or invalid value, permits implementation caps and permits earlier eviction. The checked Chromium implementation caps at two hours; that detail is version-specific.
example: Access-Control-Max-Age: 600 allows up to 10 minutes of reuse.

definition: An automatic browser OPTIONS exchange for required CORS method/header permission when no matching cached permission suffices. Successful permission gates the actual request; failure prevents that actual CORS request. Safelisted methods alone are not the complete test: header values, streaming and API flags can matter.
example: Before DELETE /v1/orders/7 from https://a.test, the browser sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method: DELETE.

definition: The browser's store of recent preflight approvals, so a matching request soon after can skip another OPTIONS round trip. Entries last at most the smaller of Access-Control-Max-Age and the browser's cap, and may be dropped sooner.

An informal term for a CORS request that avoids preflight under its full conditions: a safelisted method and header values, permitted Content-Type essence and no API/body trigger requiring preflight. Avoiding preflight does not authorize an action or expose its response to script.
example: An HTML form POST is a simple request; a POST with Content-Type: application/json is not.

definition: Fetch’s specified methods and request-header tests that can permit a CORS request without preflight. Header values have byte, syntax and length constraints, and API/body conditions also matter; merely using a listed name or method is insufficient.
example: Accept: application/json is safelisted; Authorization is not.

definition: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * permits response sharing when the request’s credentials mode is not include. Mode include requires an explicit matching origin, even if no cookie was actually sent. Other browser and server checks still apply.

An HTTP response field identifying request fields used to select a representation. A conforming cache uses it when matching stored responses; Vary: Origin is needed when Origin affects the selected CORS response header. It neither authorizes an untrusted origin nor secures private response caching by itself.
example: Without Vary: Origin, a CDN may hand the copy made for app.example to admin.example.

definition: An HTTP cache that stores responses for many users, such as a CDN or a proxy. It must never hand one user's private response to another, and needs Vary to tell header-dependent copies apart.

HTTP cache directives controlling storage, reuse and validation, such as private, no-store and max-age. Private restricts shared-cache storage while allowing private caches, which need not be only a browser. Applications must select policy appropriate to authentication and sensitive content.

An HTTP field carrying request/response metadata, such as Content-Type or Set-Cookie. HTTP/1.1 commonly displays header fields as textual name/value lines; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode fields differently, and trailer fields can follow message content.

An HTTP field identifying the representation’s media type, such as text/html or application/json. A CORS Content-Type safelist check includes the type and restrictions on the field value; strict JSON content-type handling can support a CSRF defence only with other stated conditions.
The default body format of an HTML form: name=value pairs joined with & and percent-encoded. It is CORS-safelisted, so cross-origin form posts need no preflight.
example: to=attacker&amount=500

definition: The form body format used for file uploads, splitting the body into parts. It is CORS-safelisted because an HTML form can send it.
The media type for plain text. It is CORS-safelisted, and a form with enctype="text/plain" sends name=value lines that an attacker can arrange to look like JSON.
The media type for a JSON body. It is not CORS-safelisted, so a cross-origin request with it needs a preflight, which is why requiring it helps defend JSON APIs against CSRF.
The HTML form attribute choosing how the form body is encoded: application/x-www-form-urlencoded (default), multipart/form-data or text/plain.

An HTTP request token expressing semantics such as GET, POST or DELETE. Safe semantics do not ask for application state changes, although incidental effects such as logging are allowed. Method names do not prove an implementation follows those semantics or enforces authorisation.

The HTTP method requesting a current representation of a resource. Its requested semantics are safe; incidental logging or accounting is allowed. Browsers use GET in navigation and subresource contexts, whose cookie rules differ.
The HTTP method that asks for a response's headers without the body. Like GET it is safe and CORS-safelisted.
The HTTP method for sending data to be processed, such as a form submission. It is unsafe (it can change state) but CORS-safelisted, so a cross-origin form POST needs no preflight.
The HTTP method that creates or replaces a resource with the request body. It is not CORS-safelisted, so a cross-origin PUT is preflighted.
The HTTP method for a partial change to a resource. It changes state, so it needs CSRF protection.
The HTTP method that removes a resource. It is not CORS-safelisted, so a cross-origin DELETE is preflighted.
The HTTP method that asks what a server allows. Browsers use it for CORS preflight requests; it is defined as safe.

An HTTP method whose meaning is read-only: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE. The client does not ask for any state change, though incidental effects such as logging are allowed. SameSite=Lax relies on this, so never change state on a GET.
A GET endpoint that changes data, such as GET /account/delete. It breaks the safe-method rule, and because Lax cookies ride on top-level GET navigations, a single link click can trigger it.

A three-digit status code associated with an HTTP response. In HTTP/1.1 it appears in a textual status line; newer HTTP versions encode status differently. 200 denotes success, 204 success without content, and 403 refusal to fulfil the request.

An HTTP request field carrying credentials under a scheme such as Basic or Bearer. Application JavaScript can explicitly set a bearer value, while browser-managed HTTP authentication can also supply Authorization automatically. It is not CORS-safelisted, so script-set cross-origin use requires the corresponding permission.

A token that grants access to whoever presents it, usually sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>. When page script holds it and adds it to each request, a hostile site's forged request arrives without it.

An application-defined request field such as X-Requested-With. A cross-origin CORS request using a non-safelisted author-set header needs preflight permission, which can be cached. Requiring that field helps only with strict validation, restrictive CORS and no accepted ambient-authentication bypass.

A redirect response instructing a client to request another URL, commonly via Location. Whether it is a top-level navigation depends on the initiating request; image and fetch requests can redirect too. Status and redirect context affect method rewriting and cookie eligibility.

A navigation that changes the page in the browser's address bar, such as clicking a link, a redirect or setting window.location, as opposed to loading an image, iframe or fetch inside a page. Lax cookies are sent on top-level navigations with safe methods.
A request a page makes for something it uses, such as an image, script, stylesheet or fetch, rather than a navigation to a new page. Lax cookies are not sent on cross-site subresource requests.

The HTML <script> element, which runs JavaScript written inside it (inline) or loaded from a URL with src (external). A script loaded from another site runs with your page's origin, with full access to it.
An ordinary <script> without type="module". A cross-origin classic script can load without CORS permission and runs in the including page's origin.
A JavaScript module loaded with <script type="module">. Unlike a classic script, a cross-origin module script must be allowed by CORS to load.
A <canvas> that has had a cross-origin image drawn on it without CORS approval. The browser then refuses to let script read its pixels, so the image's contents cannot leak.
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: a response header with which a resource says which origins or sites may load it in no-cors mode, for example same-site. It helps keep data out of other sites' processes.
example: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin

definition: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: a response header controlling which cross-origin resources a document may load. With require-corp, no-cors resources must come from the same origin or allow embedding with CORP; with credentialless they may load without CORP but are requested without cookies. CORS-mode requests still need CORS permission.

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: a response field whose values influence whether top-level documents share a browsing context group and retain opener relationships. Effects depend on both documents’ policies and origins; some values preserve selected popup relationships, so not every COOP header isolates every cross-origin popup.

A browser grouping of related navigable documents/windows that can hold the relevant scripting references. COOP can separate groups under defined policy rules. A group is a specification-level relationship, not a universal promise that the operating system assigns one process to it.

A family of CPU side-channel attacks disclosed in January 2018 that trick the processor's speculative execution into revealing memory. In browsers it meant a page might read cross-origin data in the same process, which led to the isolation headers.
An attack that learns secrets from indirect effects, such as timing or cache behaviour, rather than from reading them directly.

A legacy origin-domain relaxation API for cooperating documents on suitable related domains. It affects selected DOM access checks rather than every origin-based storage or API check. Modern Chrome disables the setter’s effective relaxation by default; supported exceptions and older clients need separate review.

The browser API that lets windows and iframes on different origins send each other messages. The sender should name the target origin, and the receiver should check event.origin, the source window and the message's structure.
example: child.postMessage(data, "https://widget.example")

definition: JSON with Padding: data returned inside a callback invocation and loaded as a classic script. Sensitive responses may be exposed if another page can include them with eligible credentials. A usable callback/code gadget on an allowed host can undermine an allowlist CSP; not every JSONP endpoint automatically provides arbitrary code.
example: /api/user?callback=show returns show({"name":"Ana"}).

definition: A command-line tool for making HTTP requests. It is not a browser, so the same-origin policy and CORS do not apply to it, and it can send any headers it likes.
A small Python web framework. Its examples here use request (the incoming request), session (per-user data in a signed cookie by default) and g (per-request storage).

Flask callbacks registered at application setup: before_request runs before view dispatch and can short-circuit it; after_request receives a response for modification. Exceptions, returned responses and blueprint/application scope affect which hooks run, so it is not an unconditional promise that every hook executes on every failure.
Python's standard module for security-grade randomness. secrets.token_urlsafe(n) returns n random bytes as URL-safe Base64 text, so token_urlsafe(16) gives a 128-bit value written as 22 characters.
A pattern for matching text. In origin checks, a pattern without ^ and $ anchors, or with an unescaped . (which matches any character), accepts far more than intended.
example: The regex example.com also matches https://evilexample.com and https://exampleXcom.net.

definition: An explicit list of permitted values, with everything else rejected, such as the exact origins allowed by CORS or the HTML tags a sanitiser keeps. Safer than trying to list everything bad.
example: ALLOWED = {"https://a.test"} accepts that one origin and nothing else.

definition: Single-page application: a web app that loads one page and then updates it with JavaScript, calling APIs (often on another origin) for data.
Open Worldwide Application Security Project: a non-profit that publishes free web security guidance, such as its Cheat Sheet Series and the OWASP Top 10.

OWASP's ranked list of the ten most critical web application security risk categories, updated every few years. Broken Access Control is A01 in both the 2021 and 2025 editions, and in the 2025 edition XSS falls under A05 Injection.
A family of bugs where untrusted data is mixed into code or a command without being kept separate, so the data changes what runs. SQL injection, command injection and XSS are all examples.
XSS where the payload comes in the current request, often a crafted link, and the server echoes it straight into the response.
example: /search?q=<script>...</script> reflected into the results page.

definition: XSS where the payload is saved, for example in a comment or profile, and served to everyone who views it later. No crafted link is needed, and it can spread.

XSS where the page's own JavaScript takes attacker-influenced data (a source) and writes it into a dangerous API (a sink). The unsafe flow happens in the browser, so server-side escaping does not fix it.
example: location.hash written to innerHTML.

definition: A self-spreading stored-XSS attack on MySpace in October 2005, written by Samy Kamkar. Viewing an infected profile copied the script into the viewer's own profile.
Malicious code that copies itself to new victims without anyone sending it on deliberately.
An attacker getting their own markup into your page. Even when a CSP stops inline script, injected tags such as <script src> or <base> can still cause harm.

Converting data, at the point it goes into a page, into a form that the context treats as plain data rather than code. Each context needs its own encoding: HTML text, attributes, URLs, JavaScript and CSS differ.
example: HTML escaping turns <b> into <b>, which displays as the text <b>.

definition: A character reference in HTML source, such as < for a less-than sign or ' for an apostrophe. Interpretation depends on the HTML parsing context: ordinary text and quoted attributes process these references, while script raw-text handling differs.
The Python library that Jinja2 and Flask use for HTML escaping. markupsafe.escape replaces &, <, >, " and ' with HTML entities.

Representing a byte as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits. Text may encode one character into several bytes, commonly UTF-8, before percent-encoding them. Correct handling depends on the URL component and is different from HTML escaping.
A JavaScript function that turns percent-escapes back into characters, such as %3C into <. It only decodes; the danger is where the result is written.

A source is where attacker-influenced data enters code, such as location.hash or postMessage data. A sink is an operation that is dangerous with such data, such as innerHTML or eval. A bug is a path from one to the other with no safe handling in between.
example: location.hash (source) → innerHTML (sink) is DOM XSS.

definition: DOM properties parsing markup for insertion. innerHTML replaces an element’s contents; outerHTML replaces the element itself. Inserted script elements do not execute through innerHTML, but active markup such as event handlers can still create XSS when browser policy permits it.

A DOM property replacing an element’s content with plain text instead of parsing HTML markup. Use it for text in an ordinary display element such as a paragraph. Script and style elements have active text semantics, so assigning attacker-controlled text to any element is not universally safe.
An old DOM method that writes a string of HTML straight into the page being loaded. It is an XSS sink.

JavaScript eval interprets source text; string-valued timer APIs can also compile code. Attacker-influenced source is an injection risk. An effective CSP script policy normally blocks these operations without the applicable permission; Trusted Types and newer policy mechanisms add version-specific details.

A document property exposing permitted referrer information, which may be a URL, only an origin or an empty string depending on policy and navigation. A hostile referring page can influence some values, but cannot assume its whole URL will appear.

The historically misspelled HTTP Referer request field conveying permitted referring-page information. Referrer policy can reduce or suppress it; secrets in URL query strings may leak when policy and navigation permit their inclusion.

Web Storage interfaces storing string data with origin-based access rules. localStorage can persist across sessions; sessionStorage is scoped to a page session/top-level context, with copying/restoration and browser privacy policy affecting lifetime. Neither should be treated as trusted input merely because it was stored.

An HTML attribute such as onclick or onerror whose value is handler source for its event. Injected event attributes can execute through markup insertion when allowed by browser policy. A strict nonce-based script policy without an applicable handler exception blocks them; a nonce on an element does not generally authorize its handlers.
example: runs code when the image fails to load.

definition: A URL using the javascript scheme to request script evaluation when the relevant navigation and browser policies permit it. HTML escaping does not validate this URL scheme; apply destination-appropriate URL validation and output encoding.
example: site

definition: An HTML attribute whose value is a URL, such as href on a link or src on an image or script. Values here need URL validation as well as HTML escaping.
Parsing a user-supplied URL and accepting it only if its scheme is on an approved list, such as https: and mailto:, so javascript: and data: URLs are rejected.

The urllib.parse.urlparse function splits a URL reference into components; urllib.parse is the containing Python module. Parsing alone does not validate safety or exactly reproduce browser URL interpretation.

A custom HTML data-* attribute readable through an element’s dataset. It can carry data safely when its value is encoded for a quoted ordinary attribute; the application must still avoid feeding that data into a later unsafe sink.

Jinja’s JSON serialization filter, producing markup safe for ordinary HTML text and script contexts by escaping HTML-sensitive characters. It is not safe directly inside a double-quoted HTML attribute; use a single-quoted attribute or the documented forceescape handling there.

A system producing output from a template and supplied data. Escaping defaults and contexts vary: Flask configures HTML autoescaping for selected templates, while bare Jinja needs suitable configuration. JSX is a component expression syntax with its own treatment rather than a universal HTML-template safety guarantee.
A template engine feature that HTML-escapes every inserted value unless you explicitly mark it safe. Flask turns it on for .html templates and some other extensions.
example: {{ comment.body }} in Jinja2 shows <script> as text.

definition: The Python template engine Flask uses. It writes values with {{ }} and supports filters such as |safe and |tojson.
A large Python web framework. Its templates auto-escape, and its CsrfViewMiddleware provides CSRF protection.
A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components. It escapes values written in JSX as text by default.

JavaScript syntax used with React to describe elements and properties. Ordinary string children are escaped as text rather than parsed as HTML; expressions can also produce elements, and URL/style/HTML-insertion props have separate contracts.
A Google web framework that escapes and sanitises bound values by default; bypassSecurityTrust... methods switch that off.
A JavaScript framework for user interfaces that escapes interpolated values; the v-html directive inserts raw HTML instead.

A deliberate way to switch off a safety feature for one case. In templating it is a feature such as Jinja's |safe or React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML that turns off automatic escaping for one value; each one claims the value is already safe, so reviews should check it.
A Jinja2 and Django template filter that marks a value as already-safe HTML, so auto-escaping is skipped. An escape hatch.
example: {{ bio|safe }} renders bio's HTML as-is.

definition: Django mark_safe marks data for HTML-safe handling; MarkupSafe Markup provides a related explicit trust marker in Flask/Jinja. Neither operation sanitises an arbitrary untrusted string. Their safety depends on the caller already having established the required HTML context.

Django’s helper formatting a trusted small HTML format string with conditionally escaped arguments. Ordinary untrusted arguments are escaped, while values already marked safe retain that trust; the format string and safe-marked inputs still require review.
example: format_html("{}", name)

definition: React's prop for inserting a raw HTML string into an element, bypassing JSX escaping. Its name is a warning: the value must be sanitised or provably trusted.
Vue's directive for inserting raw HTML into an element, bypassing escaping. An escape hatch.
Angular's DomSanitizer methods, such as bypassSecurityTrustHtml, that mark a value as trusted so Angular skips its sanitisation. An escape hatch.
Letting user input become part of a template itself rather than data passed into it, so the engine runs the attacker's template code, often on the server.

Cleaning untrusted input so it is safe for one particular use. For HTML, a sanitiser parses the markup and keeps only an allowlist of harmless tags and attributes. Use a maintained library, never a home-made regex.
example: DOMPurify keeps but removes 's handler.

definition: A widely used JavaScript HTML sanitiser, maintained by Cure53, that runs in the browser.
example: DOMPurify.sanitize(html) returns the cleaned HTML.

definition: A Python HTML sanitiser that wraps the Rust ammonia library; it keeps only allowlisted tags and attributes.

What you see is what you get: an editor showing formatted content while it is edited. If its output is HTML, preserve approved formatting with a maintained HTML sanitiser and review how it is inserted; not every WYSIWYG editor stores HTML.

A Python string literal starting f that inserts values in braces, such as f"

{q}

". It does no escaping, so building HTML with it is how XSS starts.

Python’s developer-oriented representation protocol for a value. repr is not a JSON serializer or an HTML/JavaScript encoder, even when a particular result happens to resemble valid JSON. Use a serializer and output-context handling appropriate to the destination.

Content Security Policy: browser-enforced policy delivered through response fields or a supported meta subset, restricting resources and selected operations. Policies can add defence against injection but do not repair unsafe output. Strict-dynamic can authorize eligible dynamically created script elements, including inline script text in addition to nonce-bearing scripts.
example: A nonce plus strict-dynamic permits matching script elements and eligible non-parser-inserted scripts; it is not a rule that every executed script carries a nonce.

definition: A named rule and arguments inside a Content Security Policy, such as script-src, frame-ancestors or require-trusted-types-for. Directives have different argument grammars and delivery restrictions; not every directive is a list of allowed resource origins.
The CSP directive that says which scripts may run: by nonce, hash, host or keyword such as 'self' or 'strict-dynamic'.
The CSP directive controlling <object> and <embed> content such as old browser plugins. object-src 'none' blocks them all.
The CSP directive controlling which URLs a <base> element may set. base-uri 'none' stops an injected <base> tag re-pointing relative script URLs.
The HTML element that sets the base URL against which relative URLs on the page are resolved. An injected one can make /app.js load from the attacker's server.

A URL reference resolved against a base URL. It may omit both scheme and host, as /app.js does, or include an authority while omitting the scheme, as //cdn.example/app.js does. Validate the parsed destination rather than assuming every relative reference stays on the original host.

A CSP source keyword matching the protected resource’s origin under CSP’s specific scheme, host and port rules. The matching rules can permit secure-scheme upgrades; it is not a universal raw-string origin comparison.

A CSP script-source keyword permitting eligible non-parser-inserted script elements in supporting browsers, including inline text under the current CSP3 matching algorithm. It also changes host/scheme source matching; eval and string-valued timers have separate checks. Trusted script builders must not consume attacker-controlled URLs or source text.
A CSP keyword allowing inline scripts and event handlers. Without an effective nonce or hash it removes most of CSP's protection against XSS; browsers ignore it when a nonce or hash is present.
A CSP keyword that allows string-to-code functions such as eval and setTimeout with a string.

A value whose required uniqueness and unpredictability depend on the protocol. Some cryptographic nonces can be counters; CSP nonces must instead be freshly generated and unguessable for each response. Uniqueness alone is not the entire CSP requirement.

A fresh unguessable value placed in a CSP nonce source and matching intended script elements. CSP Level 3 recommends at least 128 bits before encoding from a cryptographically secure generator. It authorizes matching elements, while strict-dynamic and other policy rules can also permit scripts without their own nonce, including eligible dynamically created inline script elements.
example: <script nonce="r4nd0mB64"> with script-src 'nonce-r4nd0mB64'.

definition: A script policy based on nonce or hash authorization, commonly with strict-dynamic and restrictive object-src/base-uri rules, rather than trusting a broad host list. It limits some injection paths but trusted-code gadgets, exposed nonces or unsafe application logic remain relevant.
A CSP source like 'sha256-...' that allows one exact script by the hash of its contents. Useful for static pages, where a fresh nonce per response is not possible.

A CSP nonce reused across responses instead of freshly generated. An attacker who learns it may be able to attach it to injected script markup, weakening nonce-based protection; other directives do not automatically disappear merely because the nonce is static.

A CSP script policy authorizing host or scheme sources. Its safety depends on everything reachable through those sources. Google’s 2016 sampled-policy study documented widespread bypasses involving libraries and JSONP; that historical sample is not a current universal prevalence measurement.

A script element created through the HTML parser under the specification’s parser-inserted rules. A script injected through document markup is a common example. Under the shown strict-dynamic policy a parser-inserted external script still needs applicable nonce/hash permission; programmatic insertion follows different rules.

Legitimate code in an allowed library that does something dangerous with attacker-controlled page content, for example turning certain HTML attributes into running code. Gadgets can let injected markup bypass CSP.

A CSP sent in the Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header: the browser does not enforce it but can report what it would have blocked. Used to find legitimate scripts before switching enforcement on.

A browser API and enforcement mechanism for covered injection sinks, enabled with require-trusted-types-for script in a supporting browser. Without a suitable default policy, ordinary strings at those sinks are rejected; a default policy can convert or reject them. Safety depends on policy code, permitted policy creation and subsequent use.
A Trusted Types policy named default that the browser calls automatically when a plain string reaches a protected sink, so it can convert or reject it. Without one, the string is rejected.
An error raised when a value is the wrong type for an operation, for example a plain string given to innerHTML under Trusted Types, or a non-ASCII string given to Python's hmac.compare_digest.

A generator designed to make feasible observations give negligible computational predictive advantage, under assumptions about its seed and implementation. State compromise needs separate analysis. Python secrets uses operating-system cryptographic randomness; nonce requirements still depend on the protocol.

A binary digit with two values, zero and one. Uniformly choosing n independent bits yields a space of two to the n possible strings; merely storing n bits does not ensure that much unpredictable entropy.
A group of 8 bits, which can hold 256 different values.
A way to write arbitrary bytes as text using 64 characters, each carrying 6 bits, so 3 bytes become 4 characters. The URL-safe variant uses - and _ instead of + and /.
example: 16 random bytes become 22 URL-safe Base64 characters with the = padding removed.

definition: An information-theoretic measure of uncertainty; security guessing claims require the relevant distribution and often a min-entropy bound. For a uniformly generated 128-bit secret, one independent guess succeeds with probability one in two to the power 128. Encoded text length alone does not establish that uncertainty.

A legacy response field controlling obsolete browser XSS filters. Supported current deployments should not rely on it as an XSS defence; use context-aware output handling and appropriate CSP, and check the actual clients being supported.

A separate origin or domain for untrusted user content. It reduces access to the main application’s DOM and origin-scoped data, but cookie domain scope, same-site relationships, CORS trust and credential policy must also be designed; a different origin alone does not guarantee no shared cookies.

Web application firewall: a request/response filter applying configured inspection rules. Coverage depends on what traffic it sees; ordinary HTTP request targets omit URL fragments, though applications can transmit fragment data later. A WAF is an additional control and does not repair an unsafe application sink.

A person conducting an authorised security assessment that attempts to find and demonstrate weaknesses within an agreed scope. It can be an internal or external role; being paid is not part of the technical definition.
Old native add-ons such as Flash or Java applets that pages embedded with <object> or <embed>. They had their own security holes, so strict CSPs block them with object-src 'none'.
The open-source browser project that Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge and others are built on. Its source code shows behaviour such as the 2-hour preflight-cache cap.
Google's web browser, built on Chromium. It made Lax the default for cookies without SameSite in 2020.
A CSRF attack that logs the victim into the attacker's account. Whatever the victim then saves or searches lands in an account the attacker can read, so login forms need CSRF protection too.
A CSRF variant where attacker-controlled input, such as a URL parameter, makes the real application's own JavaScript send an authenticated request. It works even when credentials are not ambient.
A program with more authority than its caller that is tricked into using that authority for the caller. In CSRF the browser is the deputy: it adds the user's cookies to the attacker's request.
An attack in which the attacker can cause an action but cannot see its result. Classic CSRF is blind because the same-origin policy stops the attacker's page reading the response.

An attacker controlling an origin that counts as same-site with a target, for example an HTTPS sibling subdomain under the same registrable domain. SameSite alone does not isolate those origins; ordinary cookie scope, credentials mode and other browser rules still determine attachment.

An unpredictable session-bound value checked on protected state-changing requests independently of ambient authentication. Under the intended origin/isolation assumptions a hostile page cannot learn it, but XSS, leakage, planting or a broken validation protocol can defeat that boundary.
example: <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="..."> in every state-changing form.

definition: The CSRF defence where the server stores a random token in the user's session and checks that every state-changing request includes the same value.
A stateless CSRF defence: the token is sent both in a cookie and in the request body or a header, and the server checks they match. The naive form fails if an attacker can plant the cookie.

OWASP's recommended double-submit variant: the token is an HMAC, under a server secret, of a random value and session-specific data. An attacker who plants a cookie cannot make a valid token for the victim's session.

Comparison designed to avoid data-dependent short-circuit matching of secret contents. Python hmac.compare_digest requires compatible types and ASCII strings or bytes-like inputs; type/length differences may still affect timing. It does not turn the surrounding request handler into a constant-time program.
A side-channel attack that measures how long an operation takes to learn a secret, such as how many leading characters of a guessed token were correct.
American Standard Code for Information Interchange: the basic 128-character set of English letters, digits and symbols. Text outside it (non-ASCII) needs Unicode.
The standard that gives a number to almost every character in every writing system, beyond ASCII's 128.

Session state retained by the server and looked up using a client session identifier, commonly in a cookie. This differs from a signed client-side session carrying the data itself; synchroniser-token designs must define where their session-bound secret is stored and validated.

Session data carried in a client cookie and authenticated by a server-held signing key, as in Flask’s default session implementation. Signing detects unauthorised changes under the scheme’s bounds but does not hide the data. Whether the application retains other server-side state is a separate design choice.
A decorator, as in Flask-Login or Django, that rejects a view's requests unless the user is logged in. It checks who the user is, not whether they meant to send this request.
Django's built-in CSRF protection, enabled in newly generated projects, which checks a token on unsafe requests.
The security framework for Java Spring applications. It enables CSRF protection by default for unsafe HTTP methods.

Sec-Fetch-* request fields supplied by supporting browsers to describe request context. Page script cannot set those forbidden names, so they can support contextual filtering, but arbitrary non-browser clients can forge them. Missing headers and permitted contexts still need independent security checks.
A Fetch Metadata request header giving the relationship between the request's initiator and its target: same-origin, same-site, cross-site or none (typed URL or bookmark).
example: Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site on a POST to /transfer is a red flag.

definition: An attack that loads your real page in an invisible iframe over a decoy, so the user's click lands on your button. CSRF tokens do not help because the click happens on your genuine page.

A CSP response-header directive controlling which ancestor origins may embed the document. None forbids embedding; nested ancestor chains are checked. It addresses framing-based clickjacking, does not inherit from default-src and is not enforced when supplied only in a meta element.
The older response header for blocking framing: DENY forbids it and SAMEORIGIN allows only your own origin. Superseded by CSP frame-ancestors but still widely sent.

A CORS request outside the conditions that avoid preflight, such as a script-set JSON content type or DELETE method. It needs applicable method/header permission, possibly reused from a matching preflight-cache entry. This differs from a simple request.

A script element without HTML’s parser-inserted status, commonly one created with document.createElement. Under the shown strict-dynamic policy, eligible external scripts and inline text in such elements can be permitted. This makes script construction with untrusted URLs or text a dangerous trust boundary.

A user-agent mode applied when a cookie omits SameSite. A client can apply Lax-like restrictions with an optional recent-cookie Lax-allowing-unsafe compatibility exception, so omission is not universally identical to explicit SameSite=Lax.

An HTTP method whose defined semantics are not safe, meaning the client may request a state change. Safe/unsafe semantics are separate from CORS-safelisted status and from whether authentication or CSRF checks are implemented.

Rules controlling whether and how much referring URL information is exposed in a request or document. A policy can reduce the value to an origin or omit it; it does not transform attacker-controlled text into trusted application data.

Text containing a character outside ASCII’s 128-character repertoire. Python hmac.compare_digest accepts ASCII-only string operands, so the illustrated guard rejects non-ASCII strings before comparing them.
